subject: English
topic: Prepositions — Fill in the Blank (Set W7)

questions.stem: She will submit the completed form _____ the deadline.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Before' means earlier than a point in time, indicating the form will be submitted prior to the deadline. 'By' could also work here (by = no later than). 'Until' indicates a continuous state up to a point. 'On' is for specific dates. 'Before the deadline' = at some time earlier than the deadline.

questions.stem: He excels _____ mathematics but struggles _____ essay writing.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Excel at' is the fixed collocation for a skill or activity: 'excel at mathematics', 'excel at chess'. 'Struggle in/with' are both used for difficulties, but 'struggle in essay writing' uses 'in' to indicate a domain. Option D reverses the prepositions incorrectly. 'Excel in' is also used but 'excel at' is more standard in competitive exams.

questions.stem: The patient was admitted _____ the hospital _____ Sunday evening.
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Admitted to the hospital' — 'to' indicates direction/destination after 'admit'. 'In' would wrongly suggest the patient was already inside. 'On Sunday evening' — 'on' is used with specific days and named time parts (on Sunday, on Monday morning). 'In the evening' is used without specifying the day.

questions.stem: She is married _____ a well-known architect and lives _____ Mumbai.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Married to' is the standard preposition — never 'married with'. 'Lives in Mumbai' — 'in' for cities/countries/large areas. 'At' is used for specific addresses or small locations. Common error: 'married with' (wrong) vs 'married to' (correct).

questions.stem: He applied _____ the post _____ Deputy Manager at the regional office.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Applied for' is the correct collocation when seeking a job, post, or permit. 'Post of Deputy Manager' uses 'of' to identify the role. 'Applied to' means submitted an application to an organisation (e.g., 'applied to the company'). Distinction: apply for = the role; apply to = the organisation.

questions.stem: The final report will be submitted _____ two weeks.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Within two weeks' = before the end of that period (any time during those two weeks). 'In two weeks' = at the end of a two-week period (a specific point). 'After two weeks' = once two weeks have passed (possibly much later). 'By two weeks' is non-standard. The intended meaning (no later than two weeks from now) is best captured by 'within'.

questions.stem: She is angry _____ her colleague _____ leaking the confidential information.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Angry with a person' is the standard collocation (not 'angry at a person' — though informal usage allows 'angry at'). 'Angry for doing something' = the reason. 'With; for' → 'angry with someone for something' is the formal/exam-standard construction. 'Angry at' is acceptable before objects/situations but not standard before persons in formal English.

questions.stem: The manager insisted _____ punctuality and insisted _____ that no one leave early.
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Insist on' is the only correct preposition for insist — 'insist on punctuality', 'insist on something'. There is no 'insist for' or 'insist in' in standard English. When followed by a clause: 'insist that + clause' (no preposition) or 'insist on + gerund'. Both blanks need 'on'.

questions.stem: She has a natural knack _____ solving complex problems and an eye _____ detail.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Knack for' = a natural talent for something. 'An eye for detail' = ability to notice details. Both collocations use 'for'. 'Knack at/with/in' are all wrong. 'Eye at' is wrong. Exam tip: fixed prepositional phrases (collocations) must be memorised — knack for, taste for, gift for, eye for, nose for.

questions.stem: He was punished _____ being late three days in a row and was suspended _____ a week.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Punished for' = reason for punishment ('for being late'). 'Suspended for a week' = duration ('for' indicating time period). Both blanks correctly use 'for'. 'Suspended from' would be used with an institution or role (e.g., 'suspended from school'), not with a time duration.
